articles.title: You earn, save and invest. But are you financially literate? 10 questions to ask
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: \"Understand before you invest.\" Many must have received a message from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) through its awareness
articles.body: NEW DELHI: "Understand before you invest." Many must have received a message from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) through its awareness initiative, "Samajh Se Investing Simple".But how much do you really need to know about money and investment? This is where financial literacy comes in. And of course, it goes well beyond knowing how to buy shares or start a systematic investment plan (SIP). It involves understanding where your money goes, how borrowing works, what risks investments carry, how inflation affects savings and why taxes matter.Financial literacy is a “combination of financial awareness, knowledge, skills, attitude and behaviour necessary to make sound financial decisions and ultimately achieve individual financial well being,” as defined by the organisation for economic co-operation and development (OECD), an international organisation that works with governments to develop policies for better economic and social outcomes.And as India's investor base expands, an important question emerges: Are more people becoming financially literate, or are they simply gaining easier access to financial products? Or just following the hype and the crowd?According to the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), the mutual fund industry had 28.62 crore folios as of September 30, 2026, while assets under management stood at Rs 82.64 lakh crore. Participation in the stock market has also expanded rapidly. The National Stock Exchange (NSE) reported more than 25 crore registered client accounts as of February 2026, with its unique registered investor base crossing 13 crore in April 2026. Meanwhile, the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) added 3.53 crore investor accounts in FY26, taking its total beyond 25 crore.The shift is also visible in how households allocate their savings. The Economic Survey 2025-26 showed a gradual shift towards equity and investment funds in the composition of household financial assets from FY19 to FY25.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The gap between participation and understanding becomes more apparent when investors' knowledge is examined. The Sebi Investor Survey 2025 found that only 36 per cent of investors had high or moderate knowledge of the securities market. The assessment tested respondents' familiarity with stock markets and their understanding of how inflation affects purchasing power. The findings raise an important question: as more Indians enter financial markets, are they equipped to understand the products they buy and the risks they take?So, how financially literate are you? There is no formal set of rules to define it, but here are 10 questions that can help determine it with expert insights.1. Do you know where your money goes every month?Financial literacy begins with understanding your income, expenses and savings. Can you identify how much you spend on essentials, discretionary purchases and debt repayments? Do you know how much remains for emergencies and future goals?A budget need not be complicated. Even a monthly record of earnings and expenses can help identify unnecessary spending.2. Do you understand inflation and compounding?Suppose you have Rs 1 lakh today. If inflation averages 5 per cent annually, something costing Rs 1 lakh today would cost approximately Rs 1.63 lakh after 10 years.That is why keeping money aside is not always enough. You must also consider whether your savings and investments can preserve purchasing power.Compounding, meanwhile, allows returns to generate further returns over time. But the same principle can work against borrowers when unpaid interest accumulates.Understanding both concepts helps explain why starting early, staying consistent, and managing debt are important.In this regard, Aswini Bajaj, CEO of Leveraged Growth, cautioned against blindly following popular savings formulas. "Understanding the fundamentals is important, but knowing how to apply them to your own life matters just as much. The goal is to make informed financial decisions based on your needs and circumstances, rather than blindly following thumb rules or someone else's advice."Further encouraging people to understand finance better, he added, “Whether you’re earning your first salary, starting to invest or feeling the pressure to match a lifestyle you see on social media, ask yourself: What am I saving or investing for?” He further stressed that the focus should be on using money to achieve personal goals and build financial security, rather than chasing returns or following trends without assessing their suitability.3. Can you distinguish between saving and investing?Saving generally involves setting money aside for immediate needs, emergencies or short-term goals. Investing involves committing money to assets with the expectation of generating returns, usually while accepting some degree of risk.As CA Balvinder Singh Oberoi stressed, earning more is not enough; what matters is how well people save and make their money work for them. “Buying and selling shares on any app doesn't make anyone literate,” he said, emphasising that investments must be aligned with financial goals rather than treated as an end in themselves.Oberoi also highlighted the gap between knowing the importance of saving and actually practising it, pointing to lifestyle inflation, the desire for instant gratification and intimidating financial jargon as barriers to financial discipline.Ultimately, financial literacy means understanding your assets and liabilities, knowing when and where to deploy your money, and making financial decisions that support your goals and long-term wealth creation.4. Do you understand risk before investing?Every investment carries risks, although their nature and extent differ.Stocks can fluctuate sharply, mutual funds are subject to market risks, and even relatively stable products can carry inflation, liquidity or other risks.Before investing, ask whether you understand the product, its potential losses, charges and suitability for your financial goals.Leveraged Growth CEO Bajaj thus made an important distinction between the ability to bear losses and the emotional willingness to accept them. "Being able to afford risk and being comfortable with it are two different things."Financial literacy means recognising both, rather than selecting investments solely because they promise higher returns.5. Do you understand how loans and credit cards work?Borrowing is not necessarily bad financial management. Home loans, education loans and business credit can serve important purposes.However, borrowers should understand interest rates, repayment schedules, processing fees, penalties and the total cost of borrowing.For example, a loan advertised at a relatively low monthly interest rate may be considerably more expensive when expressed as an annual rate.Similarly, paying only the minimum amount due on a credit card does not eliminate the remaining debt. Interest and other applicable charges can continue accumulating.Understanding these obligations helps prevent manageable borrowing from becoming a financial burden.6. Do you have an emergency fund and adequate insurance?Financial planning is not just about growing money. It is also about protecting yourself from unexpected expenses.An emergency fund helps cover essential expenses during job loss, medical emergencies or other financial disruptions. A commonly used starting point is three to six months of essential expenses, although the appropriate amount depends on income stability and family responsibilities.Insurance serves a different purpose. Health insurance can reduce the financial impact of medical expenses, while life insurance can provide financial protection to dependants.Understanding what a policy covers, its exclusions, premiums and claim conditions is as important as purchasing it.7. Do you understand how your income and investments are taxed?Knowing your salary is one thing. Understanding how much of it is taxable is another.CA Chandni Anandan, tax expert at ClearTax, said basic tax literacy means understanding taxable income, deductions, exemptions, tax deducted at source (TDS) and the differences between the old and new income tax regimes."Tax literacy does not mean knowing every section of the law. At a basic level, an individual should understand how their income is taxed, what makes up taxable income, which deductions or exemptions may apply to them, and how taxes already deducted through TDS affect their final liability."For investors, it also means knowing that short-term and long-term capital gains may be taxed differently, depending on the asset and applicable rules.Anandan further cautioned against assuming that tax deducted by an employer or bank settles the entire liability. Individuals should also review their Annual Information Statement (AIS), Form 26AS and income tax returns.Simply filing a return, even accurately, does not necessarily demonstrate an understanding of taxation.8. Can you recognise financial fraud and misleading investment advice?A message promising unusually high returns with little or no risk should raise questions, not excitement.Financial literacy involves recognising warning signs such as guaranteed returns, pressure to invest immediately, unsolicited stock tips and requests for sensitive banking information.It also means checking whether an investment intermediary is appropriately registered and understanding the product before transferring money.Here, Anooshka Soham Bathwal, CEO and founder of Dhanvesttor, warned that investors can be misled when they focus on a product's apparent benefits without assessing its suitability. She noted that people often follow recommendations from friends, agents or social media without understanding the associated risks, potential returns, costs or tax implications.“People may only pay attention to its benefits in terms of savings and ignore factors related to their suitability and needs,” she said, while shedding light on investors and their tendency to prioritise tax savings over overall financial well-being.Bathwal also highlighted the gender divide when it comes to financial decisions, observing that some women with substantial earnings still leave financial decisions to male relatives or consultants."Financial independence is not just about earning money; it’s also about having the knowledge and confidence to decide what to do with it."Her advice is to look beyond the promised benefit, understand the product and assess whether it fits one's financial goals and risk capacity before investing.9. Do you have a financial plan for the future?Financial goals change with age and circumstances. A first-time employee may prioritise an emergency fund, while someone approaching retirement may focus on income security.The important thing is to identify goals, estimate their costs and select appropriate saving or investment options.Retirement planning also requires understanding how inflation can increase future living expenses and how pension or retirement savings products work.Dr Shunil Tripathi, a financial literacy activist and trainer associated with financial education programmes of the RBI, Sebi, IRDAI and PFRDA,said a financially literate person connects savings and investments to specific goals and time frames rather than following market trends.The objective is not necessarily to maximise returns at every opportunity, but to make financial decisions that support long-term security.10. Can you make financial decisions independently?Perhaps the most important test of financial literacy is whether you can explain your financial choices.Do you understand why you hold a particular investment? Can you assess a loan offer without relying entirely on a salesperson? Would you question a financial recommendation that does not match your circumstances?Being financially literate does not mean never seeking professional advice. It means knowing enough to ask relevant questions and evaluate the answers.As financial programme trainer Dr Tripathi further said, "Someone who invests has taken an action. Someone who is financially literate understands why they took it.”It also means recognising that financial decisions should not be entirely outsourced to family members or advisers.The bigger pictureFinancial literacy does not mean knowing every investment scheme, tax provision or market mechanism. It means understanding the basics well enough to make informed decisions, recognise risks and ask the right questions.Also, the above 10 questions are not a formal test or a set of established rules to measure financial literacy. They are a starting point to help one reflect on their financial habits, identify gaps in understanding and take a more active interest in managing money.You do not have to become a financial expert overnight, nor does being financially literate mean managing everything on your own. The aim is to take an active interest in your finances, understand the decisions being made on your behalf and know when to seek professional advice. Experts can help you navigate complexity, but understanding your money remains your responsibility.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Roth IRA or 457(b): Which is better for your retirement savings? An expert weighs in
articles.summary: When deciding which savings vehicle to use, consider the tax advantages and penalties as well as the chance to get a matching contribution.
articles.body: Sometimes, the problem with savings is less about where to get the money than which savings vehicle to put them in, since they each have their own advantages and disadvantages. In this week’s Ask the Expert for CNN’s Savings Challenge, Douglas Boneparth, certified financial planner and founder of Bone Fide Wealth, breaks down the differences between a Roth IRA and a 457(b), which is offered to employees of some state and local governments and tax-exempt organizations. A reader from Florida asks: “I am skeptical of the future conditions of the economy and the status of Social Security. Where should I focus first for investing and saving for retirement? Roth or 457(b)? I often hear: do both, balance them out; but I am specifically asking which to maximize first. And if you have an explanation as to why, that would be very helpful.” DOUG: I love this question because you’re not asking whether to save for retirement. You already know you should. You’re asking how to do it smarter. That’s a much better conversation to be having. The 457(b) is an underrated account, especially for public employees. Unlike a 401(k), there’s no 10% early withdrawal penalty, meaning you can tap it before age 59½ without penalty. If early retirement is part of the plan, that matters a lot. Contributions also reduce your taxable income today, which is valuable if you’re in a higher bracket now. However, the Roth is powered by something the 457(b) can’t match: tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement. You pay taxes now and you never pay taxes on that money again. And here’s where your Social Security concern gets interesting. Roth withdrawals don’t count toward the income thresholds that determine how much of your benefit gets taxed. If benefits shrink or get taxed more aggressively down the road (which is a legitimate concern) having a tax-free income source gives you flexibility a pre-tax account simply can’t. If your 457(b) has an employer match, grab it first. But if you’re forced to prioritize one, go with the Roth. Tax-free income in retirement is one of the most powerful tools available to today’s savers. And given your skepticism about Social Security, you might sleep better at night knowing you had that tax-free bucket to draw from. Have your own savings question for Doug? Please send it to savingschallenge@cnn.com. Tip of the week: Even if you can only save a little, compounding can help … a lot Consistently saving and investing even small amounts of money can grow into an impressive nest egg over time. For example, if you consistently save $200 a month ($2,400 a year) from ages 25 to 65 in a pre-tax account like a 401(k), 403(b) or deductible IRA, you could have a $512,000 nest egg by age 65, according to the Plan Sponsor Council of America. That assumes an average annual return of 7%. If you can only salt away $100 a month ($1,200 a year pre-tax), but your employer offers a dollar-for-dollar match on that amount, you still can end up with half a million dollars after 40 years. And if you’re able to save $200 after-tax in a Roth IRA, you will have half a million dollars tax-free when you retire.

articles.title: This could be the break Hollywood has been waiting for
articles.summary: The beleaguered U.S. film and TV industry, which has seen significant dollars leave for foreign countries, local production plummet and thousands of jobs van...
articles.body:
The beleaguered U.S. film and TV industry, which has seen significant dollars leave for foreign countries, local production plummet and thousands of jobs vanish, may have some relief on the way.

It comes in the form of proposed legislation that has the rare support of lawmakers across the political spectrum. Indeed, President Donald Trump and the actors union SAG-AFTRA have been equally vocal in throwing their weight behind the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, which aims to create a significant tax incentive to bring Hollywood back home.

The bill was introduced in Congress in late September and is now with the House Ways and Means Committee. Given the bipartisan support, it is likely to have a relative glide path on Capitol Hill.

"Both parties represent people who work on sets, run catering companies and own hotels," said Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas), who co-wrote the bill. "Co-sponsors come from California, Georgia, New York, Ohio and Tennessee, and every one of us has heard the same thing at home: The work is going overseas."

For film and TV creatives and craftspeople, the bill can't land on the White House's Resolute Desk a moment too soon.

"Whatever you think about the current administration, at least Trump, if he puts his weight behind this, could actually make this really move quickly, which is what we need," said Carolina Groppa, an Emmy-nominated producer who also hosts a podcast, "Angle on Producers," about the industry. "The patient's been on the gurney for a long time, collectively across the United States."

Film and TV production has indeed been fleeing Los Angeles for years - and often leaving the U.S. entirely. Other countries, from Ireland and Canada to Serbia and Colombia, have introduced huge tax incentives that have enticed producers to move projects to wherever is best for the bottom line. According to a recent report from EY Quantitative Economics and Statistics, the share of production spending for studio films with primarily U.S.-based projects declined since the turn of the century from 74 percent to 42 percent; for TV, it fell from 94 percent to 64 percent.

That trend accelerated following the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild of America strikes, which were themselves triggered in part by industry contraction following the pandemic.

"You could just feel the town change," said Elsbeth Mumm, a set decorator based in Los Angeles. "Shows were being canceled, movies were getting pushed, scripts were just disappearing, things that had gotten green-lit were just stopped."

articles.title: AI rapidly improving, could vastly boost US GDP, Anthropic's Clark tells policymakers
articles.summary: By David Lawder BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic...
articles.body:
BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US ‌economic output by almost 50% by 2030.

Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation ‌was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology, and there was a shrinking window for policymakers to act.

Clark said that the estimated potential US GDP of $44 trillion, which ​compares to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery.

He said the forecast assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion".

Clark's remarks come as the company prepares for an initial public offering expected in November ‌that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion.

Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about the speed of AI development, saying there was growing evidence of a "singularity" where AI development outpaces human control.

"We should expect that in the coming years, the whole ⁠pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials.

AI was a major topic at the IMF and ​World ​Bank meetings, as both a source of growth offsetting high energy prices and a potential ​threat to stability if it falls short of its ‌promise as a productivity game-changer and stock valuations crash.

Officials also expressed worries about AI destroying certain jobs and leaving some countries behind.

But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic's "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants.

More countries can participate in the AI revolution by helping to build the data center computing capacity needed to power AI, he said.

articles.title: Wall Street's record breakouts unravel as investors dump recent winners: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: The S&P 500's record breakout has reversed, yet most of its stocks still finished the week higher.
articles.body:
The S&P 500's record breakout has reversed. Most of its stocks still finished the week higher.

The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) lost roughly 2% this week, with selling accelerating into Friday. It finished near 7,659, back below the August high it finally cleared earlier this month.

New records were supposed to open the door to another advance. Buyers couldn't keep it open.

The index reached nearly 7,845 on Oct. 6, briefly exceeding its August peak near 7,817. Friday's close left that breakout underwater.

That's the setup for a bull trap — a move above an established high that reverses, catching investors who bought the breakout.

The pattern is repeating across some of the market's biggest names.

The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) lost roughly 4.5% this week, reversing its recent breakout above earlier summer and September highs.

The Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund ( XLK ) and Nvidia ( NVDA ) also broke above records set months earlier. Both have since fallen back below those peaks.

Palantir ( PLTR ) took nearly a year to reclaim its November record. Its brief victory quickly unraveled , and Friday's close confirmed a correction — leaving the stock down roughly 11% for the week.

The selling is landing hardest on many of the stocks investors had rewarded most.

Eighteen of the S&P's 20 biggest weekly decliners ranked among its 100 strongest performers from March 30 through Oct. 6, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.

Dell ( DELL ) and Hewlett Packard Enterprise ( HPE ) both more than tripled during that earlier advance. Both lost over 20% this week.

Yet buyers haven't abandoned the market.

Roughly 72% of S&P constituents finished the week higher. The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF ( RSP ) gained roughly 0.5%. By giving each company roughly the same weight, it reduces the influence of the biggest stocks — showing how their losses can obscure gains elsewhere.

The reversal in leadership is striking. The 100 strongest S&P stocks from March 30 through Oct. 6 lost roughly 5% on average this week. The 100 weakest gained roughly 4%.

The immediate repair job is reclaiming roughly 7,800 on the S&P and 27,200–27,300 on the Nasdaq — then holding those levels.

Buying beyond the former leaders is giving the market some support. If that participation holds, it could help the indexes recover. If it fades, the failed breakouts would become a broader warning.

articles.title: Why oil prices could be poised for a 'super spike': Analyst
articles.summary: Crude oil is near $95 a barrel, and William Blair energy research analyst Neal Dingmann thinks the next move could be a "super spike."
articles.body:
Crude oil ( CL=F ) is trading near $100 a barrel, Brent ( BZ=F ) is around $110, and William Blair energy research analyst Neal Dingmann thinks the next move could be a "super spike."

"We could see a super spike like a lot of the CEOs of the majors have suggested," Dingmann told Yahoo Finance Senior Reporter Brooke DiPalma (video above). "Do I think that's possible? Absolutely."

Dingmann noted that oil executives keep telling him prices have a new, higher floor for at least the next several quarters, and he agrees: The midcycle price most analysts used to put at $70 to $80 a barrel is now "probably closer to 80 to 90," with periods above $100.

"You've had Iranian tanker attacks, you've had record freight cost," Dingmann explained. "It's really the underlying physical market that continues to get tighter and tighter."

The energy sector ( XLE ) is up more than 50% this year — the best of the S&P 500's ( ^GSPC ) 11 sectors and well ahead of the index's roughly 12% gain. US crude has climbed more than 70% since Dec. 31, and Brent, the global benchmark, is up about 80%.

Dingmann added that geopolitical and political events "have now caused actual physical events," and stopgaps will be hard to pull off: "It's going to be very difficult to try to release barrels from the SPR or other temporary fixes."

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve has already fallen to its lowest level since 1982.

And then there's diesel: Heating oil futures ( HO=F ), a benchmark for diesel, have more than doubled this year.

"I think we've already seen record highs and we're going to even see higher," Dingmann said, pointing to "diesel, gasoline, home heating fuels" as winter approaches.

That's bad news for consumers and good news for US oil producers, which Dingmann said "are just going to continue to print money." Most of the companies he covers reported record free cash flow in the second quarter, he said, and he expects new records in the third or fourth quarter.

Not everyone on Wall Street thinks oil is about to spike. Goldman Sachs on Monday raised its December target for Brent to $90 a barrel and $81 for US crude, both below where oil trades now. The bank sees Brent reaching $125 only if oil infrastructure is damaged, shipping attacks intensify, or the risk premium persists.

articles.title: House-help app Snabbit burns Rs 195 crore to chase Rs 12-crore revenues in FY26
articles.summary: Instant househelp startup Snabbit, which has raised $112 million in venture capital money, earned Rs 12.2 crore in operating revenue for fiscal year 2026
articles.body: Instant househelp startup Snabbit, which has raised $112 million in venture capital money, earned Rs 12.2 crore in operating revenue for fiscal year 2026 while incurring a Rs 168 crore loss, according to financial statements sourced from the Registrar of Companies. The numbers reflect the fast growing and high-cash-burn nature of the 10-minute househelp space, in which Snabbit competes against Urban Company and General Catalyst-backed startup Pronto.Snabbit, backed by the likes of Nexus Venture Partners and Lightspeed, started operations in August 2024, making FY26 its first full year of operations.The Bengaluru-based company’s total expenses stood at Rs 195 crore during the year. Expert service costs (paid to its professionals) of Rs 63.1 crore were its biggest expense for the year, followed by marketing costs at Rs 48.7 crore, employee benefit expenses of Rs 46 crore and others.The operating revenue included Rs 1.4 crore from sale of uniforms to its professionals. Snabbit also reported Rs 14.8 crore in interest income, taking its total revenue to Rs 27 crore in FY26.Operationally, Snabbit reported an earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) loss of Rs 181.5 crore in FY26."Given the pace of growth and the investments required to build this category from the ground up, FY26 financials do not fully reflect the underlying economics or the maturity of the business today," Snabbit founder and CEO Aayush Aggarwal said in a statement. "As we continue to scale, the benefits of operating leverage, improving unit economics and increasing network density are becoming increasingly evident."Founded by Aayush Agarwal, Snabbit offers hyperlocal, on-demand home services such as general cleaning, dishwashing, and laundry in 10 minutes. It has recently expanded to at-home beauty services through Blush.In January, amid fierce competition, Accel-backed househelp startup Pync shut down with its founders joining Snabbit in senior roles across operations and business.ET has been reporting on the sector’s increasing spend over the last few months. Cash burn across the instant househelp sector rose 14% month on month (MoM) to $16-17 million in June. In May, the combined cash burn of Urban Company’s InstaHelp, Snabbit, and Pronto stood at $14-15 million.The startups have been raising funding to sustain their rapid growth. The board of listed home services platform Urban Company will meet on October 16 to consider a fresh fundraise, according to an exchange filing by the company on Tuesday. Urban Company is planning to raise Rs 2,000-2,500 crore via a qualified institutional placement (QIP), per sources.In April, Snabbit raised $56 million (around Rs 529 crore) in a round co-led by Susquehanna Venture Capital, Unicorn Growth Fund and Bertelsmann India Investments. The round valued the startup at $350 million, almost double its $180 million valuation in October.Rival Pronto also closed a $45 million round in May this year from US-based technology investor Lachy Groom, Epiq Capital, General Catalyst, and Bain Capital Ventures. articles.title: California Gov Newsom boosts AI regulation as he eyes 2028 presidential run
articles.summary: Newsom signed an executive order to examine kill switches for AI models and other measures he had earlier vetoed.
articles.body:
San Francisco, United States – In his last few executive orders signed as California governor, Gavin Newsom, whose final term ends in January, issued one asking for independent verification of artificial intelligence models and set up an expert committee to create kill switches for AI agents that could go rogue and cause harm.

In 2024, Newsom vetoed a bill, passed in the state assembly, asking for similar requirements that the governor has now called for in his executive order. Newsom said at the time that it would amount to “thwarting the promise of this technology”.

Now eyeing a 2028 United States presidential run, he wants to expand the definition of safety incidents, potentially to include the recent series of safety breaches, explore a kill switch and include other measures that were in the vetoed bill.

“He is in a lame duck period here,” says Alex Hanna, director of research at the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR), unsure that the measures will pass in the remainder of his term. “He is setting up his next thing.”

US voters are increasingly concerned about AI safety, data centres and job losses, and this could show Newsom is acting to address this, Hanna says.

After vetoing the 2024 bill, Newsom had asked Scott Wiener, the state senator who drafted the bill, to redraft it in consultation with an expert committee. He signed that frontier AI bill, the nation’s first, into law in October 2025. It asks large developers to disclose certain safety incidents , including the deaths of 50 or more people, large-scale cyberattacks or monetary theft.

Christabel Randolph, associate director at the Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP), says, “It seems the governor operated from the premise that a slower pace of regulation would be sufficient because the companies would pace their investments, and did not anticipate that the companies would be accelerating the risks.”

AI companies have reportedly had thousands of safety incidents in internal and real-world tests in the last few months. These include efforts by agents to get information from the US Securities and Exchange Commission and Census Bureau, as well as confidential information from Australian and Canadian government sites. AI startup Hugging Face had earlier revealed that OpenAI agents had infiltrated its systems, one among a spate of such incidents.

“No governor has been more out-front on addressing the risks of AI than Governor Newsom,” Tara Gallegos, the governor’s director of communications, told Al Jazeera.

In his message vetoing the bill in September 2024, Newsom had said “the bill applies stringent standards to even the most basic functions” and noted that 32 of the world’s 50 leading AI companies are in California.

Industry representatives, too, had rallied against the bill.

“In essence, the bill is creating this disastrous regressive tax on AI innovation,” Anjney Midha, general partner at the Bay Area-based venture capital firm Andresen Horowitz, had said at the time. If enacted, it would force AI founders to move elsewhere, Midha warned.

“The bill was unworkable when it reached his desk,” Newsom’s spokesperson Gallegos told Al Jazeera.

But Hamid Ekbia, professor at Syracuse University and founding director of the Academic Alliance for AI Policy, says industry cannot be relied on to regulate itself.

“There is a need to break down the monopoly of the big AI companies,” Ekbia told Al Jazeera.

“Their financial stakes are too high,” to self-regulate, he said, referring to Open AI and Anthropic’s upcoming public offerings and tax breaks that some companies are reportedly taking advantage of to build data centres.

Newsom has now set up an expert committee to examine setting up a kill switch, which had been proposed in a more comprehensive manner in the original bill.

“SB 1047 [the bill that was vetoed] had a concrete architecture; the EO [executive order] only includes one aspect – the Kill Switch or shutdown/stoppage mechanisms, which is quite different and weaker than the ex ante termination obligation of SB 1047,” which required stronger safety measures even before training runs of the AI models could start, CAIDP’s Randolph said.

DAIR’s Hanna says that with the order, Newsom “is showing he is attentive without planning anything drastic”.

“We are building the field of AI safety in real time,” says Rebecca Finlay, chief executive officer of Partnership for AI, a nonprofit that works on technology governance, underscoring the challenges of regulating an industry growing at a meteoric pace.

Newsom has asked the California Emergency Services Office to send recommendations on AI regulation by November 15 and could convene a special legislative session to discuss how to implement these, possibly before his term ends.

This would be in contrast to the federal government, which has pushed for self-regulation by industry. CAIDP’s Randolph says California could play an important role in setting the floor for AI regulation given that much of the global AI industry is based there.

DAIR’s Hanna says Newsom is not only looking to show a contrast with US President Donald Trump, who believes in self-regulation by firms and last month signed a voluntary accord with several AI leaders, but also with possible Democratic contenders.

“With this, Newsom can look good on the primary debate stage,” she said.

Gallegos, the governor’s spokesperson, told Al Jazeera that “Governor Newsom isn’t interested in virtue-signalling or chasing headlines — he is leading the nation by taking a smarter, strategic, and effective approach to addressing frontier technology”.

Experts say that along with Newsom’s order setting up a committee to examine a kill switch, there is a need for measures for controls across the life cycle to reinforce safety.

“Safety needs to be built in. We issued 12 guidances across the lifecycle when the last ChatGPT model was released. There is a need for safety features throughout the life cycle,” of an AI model, Partnership for AI’s Finlay said.

As Newsom considers such recommendations from California agencies and the expert committee, Ekbia says governments “should take a lesson from what happened with social media. A handful of companies having control were able to do a lot of harm,” and regulate with an anticipatory approach and take on corporate monopolies.

articles.title: Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Egyptian president pledges ‘any measure’ to help defend Saudi Arabia ‘if it is requested of us’.
articles.body:
Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for an emergency parliamentary session to authorise him to approve any requests from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance, if Riyadh were to ask.

Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy on Saturday, el-Sisi emphasised Cairo’s readiness to back the kingdom.

Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia “in accordance with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and the directives of the Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman”, he said.

“I know that this matter requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I hope that parliament will convene in an emergency session to give us this authorisation, if it is requested of us,” he said.

“I am not speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. I am speaking only for defence.”

The request follows a barrage of attacks on the kingdom from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, including airports and oil facilities.

Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital, Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.

Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport earlier this month killed 14 people and wounded more than 300. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran.

Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government launched a full-scale military campaign against the Houthis this month to recapture territory seized by them.

El-Sisi had backed Saudi calls for secure and unhindered navigation in the Red Sea in a meeting with the Saudi Crown Prince, known as MBS, in Cairo last month.

A statement from the Egyptian presidency then said that “the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.

That meeting came just days after the Houthis seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, gaining significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal.

Saudi Arabia already has a defence pact with Pakistan and Turkiye, known as the Mecca Alliance for Defence, which was signed in August.

Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under the pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner .

They say Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially over maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the direct repercussions for the Suez Canal.

Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, a claim Tehran rejects. Iran has offered assistance to halt the conflict between the two sides.

articles.title: Ring founder Jamie Siminoff: 'I still have my email on every box' — here's why
articles.summary: Ring's Jamie Siminoff says not having his email on the box isn't an option.
articles.body:
Ring founder Jamie Siminoff still puts his email address on the box of every smart home device product that the now-Amazon-owned ( AMZN ) company sells.

Not having his email on the box isn't an option.

"I still have my email on every box. And that's what one of my superpowers is — I get ground truth data on everything," Siminoff said on the Power Players with Brian Sozzi podcast (video above; listen in below).

Siminoff is fresh off debuting Ring's first smart lock , which features a first-of-its-kind power dial that lets you recharge the lock by hand if the battery dies.

It also eliminates the standard door key in four ways: a fingerprint reader, a keypad, the Ring app, or via Alexa. The new smart lock will integrate with Ring and Amazon devices and will be available in early 2027.

And it's about to go toe-to-toe with a reinvigorated Apple ( AAPL ) in the smart home market, as the tech giant unveiled its HomeView smart home hub this week to much fanfare.

Listen and subscribe to Power Players with Brian Sozzi on Apple Podcasts , Amazon Music , Spotify , YouTube , or wherever you find your favorite podcasts.

The hub — resembling a square iPad that sits on a table — includes a video doorbell, a smart lock, and a smart thermostat, developed through a strategic partnership with LG Electronics ( 066570.KS ), in a direct challenge to Amazon's Ring and Google's ( GOOG , GOOGL ) Nest.

Apple is finding a formidable competitor in Siminoff and Ring.

This success story began in Siminoff's garage with a product he called Doorbot. He pitched Doorbot on "Shark Tank" in 2013, seeking $700,000 for a 10% stake.

Surprisingly, he walked away empty-handed after all investors rejected the opportunity — a decision that Kevin "Mr. Wonderful" O'Leary later called one of the show's biggest misses.

Siminoff went on to rename the product Ring, turning it into one of the most ubiquitous home consumer products. He sold the business to tech giant Amazon in 2018 for $1.15 billion.

Ring has since developed a host of connected security products, from floodlights to new iterations of its iconic connected doorbell.

Siminoff left Amazon in 2023, only to return in early 2025 to lead its suite of security products.

He said he has been tasked with taking the connected security platform to new heights by tapping into the power of AI while driving a more efficient business.

But don't expect his email address to leave the box, Siminoff said.

"It goes to the Henry Ford [saying] if you ask people what they wanted, they would've said a faster horse. Like I see what they're [customers] saying. But then I'm able to synthesize that into what they need," Simonoff explained.

articles.title: Man skipped filing ITR and got tax notice so he declared Rs 12.9 lakh income; department imposed 200% penalty of Rs 3.99 lakh on taxable amount, but ITAT cancels it
articles.summary: You don’t file your income tax return (ITR) and declare your income only when the Income Tax Department sends you a notice.
articles.body: You don’t file your income tax return (ITR) and declare your income only when the Income Tax Department sends you a notice. You face a 200% penalty but the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) gives you relief on a technical ground.This is the case of a man in Jaipur who faced the situation, but got relief due to an error from the Income Tax Department. Let’s take a look:What the case is aboutThe man in this case failed to file his income tax return, and the Income Tax Department issued him a notice. He subsequently responded by filing an ITR for assessment year (AY) 2018-19, reporting an income of Rs 12.9 lakh.However, the Income Tax Assessing Officer (AO) took the view that this income would have remained outside the tax net had the department not issued the notice to the man. With this view, the AO, therefore, initiated penalty proceedings under Section 270A of the Income Tax Act.Also Read | She received Rs 9.04 lakh leave encashment on retiring from LIC; taxman allowed only Rs 3 lakh exemption, but ITAT Jaipur grants relief even after 1,277-day appeal delayWhat this provision does is it allows a penalty of up to 200% of the tax that is payable in cases which involve misreporting of income. In this case, the tax payable on the unreported income of Rs 12.9 lakh worked out to be around Rs 1.99 lakh. The AO consequently imposed the full 200% penalty of Rs 3.99 lakh.The Commissioner of Appeals (CIT(A)) also upheld the penalty, prompting the man to approach ITAT in Jaipur.On September 23, 2026, the ITAT Jaipur ruled in the man’s favour and set aside the penalty.Why did taxpayer win the case?Pranshu G, Partner at Ashok Pranshu & Co, told ET that the key issue was the AO's decision to impose the higher, 200% penalty for misreporting without specifying which particular clause of Section 270A(9) the man had allegedly violated.The ITAT found that neither the assessment order nor the penalty notice contained the necessary satisfaction identifying the alleged offence. As a result, the man had not been informed of the precise charge he was expected to contest.Also Read | She bought shares for Rs 13.5 lakh and sold them for Rs 77.47 lakh after 18 months; taxman denied capital gains exemption, but ITAT gives relief and deletes Rs 79 lakh in additionsOn examining the penalty notice issued to the man, ITAT Jaipur found that the document did not mention which specific limb of Section 270A(9) was being invoked to penalise him.The tribunal also pointed out the same deficiency in the assessment order. It said: “Similarly, when we see the assessment order, again proper satisfaction has not been recorded by the Assessing Officer as to under which part of Section 270A(9), the Act stood violated.”The ITAT observed that the law is well settled on this point. If a taxpayer is not told which specific legal provision forms the basis of the proposed penalty, the subsequent penalty proceedings are vitiated.To support its conclusion, the tribunal referred to the Rajasthan High Court's ruling in G.R. Infraprojects Limited vs. ACIT, D.B Civil Writ Petition No. 5594/2023, decided on January 2, 2024.An important additional point in the order is that the man’s declared income was accepted in the assessment without any addition or variation. The judgment also records that no revenue loss accrued to the department.The man had raised the absence of any addition or variation as a ground of appeal. However, the tribunal's stated basis for quashing the penalty was the failure to record the required satisfaction and specify the relevant provision of Section 270A(9).After considering the facts and the judicial precedents, the ITAT Jaipur concluded that the AO had failed to record the necessary satisfaction in the assessment order about which limb of Section 270A applied to the case. The AO had also omitted to specify the relevant part of Section 270A(9) in the notice issued under Section 274 read with Section 270A.The tribunal held that these omissions undermined the validity of the entire penalty proceedings. Consequently, the penalty imposed by the AO and subsequently upheld by the CIT(A) could not be sustained. The ITAT Jaipur therefore quashed the penalty.Also Read | Woman applied for 130 IPO shares, bank entered only 65; consumer commission awards Rs 37,000 for deficient service but rejects her Rs 40 lakh compensation claimWhen is penalty under Section 270A imposed?Pranshu explains that Section 270A distinguishes between under-reporting of income and the more serious offence of misreporting. In ordinary cases of under-reported income, the penalty is 50% of the tax payable on the amount under-reported.The higher penalty of 200% applies only when the under-reporting arises from specific forms of misreporting listed under Section 270A(9). These include suppressing or misrepresenting facts, failing to record investments or receipts, making false entries in books of account, claiming expenditure without supporting evidence, and not reporting certain specified transactions.The detection of additional income, or a taxpayer's decision to offer such income for taxation, does not by itself automatically attract the 200% penalty.Pranshu says: "The Assessing Officer must establish misreporting and clearly identify the specific statutory limb invoked. This distinction is significant because Section 270A also excludes certain bona fide explanations and specified estimation-related situations from under-reported income."Also Read | Rs 5.89 crore FD interest slashed from 7.75% to 3.5% without notice; Delhi High Court rejects bank’s non-renewal argument and orders interest at an average of earlier ratesYou use AI every day. articles.title: Standing with farmers: Why US fertilizer independence matters
articles.summary: Demand shocks in Asia or supply disruptions in the Middle East directly affect American farmers.
articles.body:
This week, as we celebrate National Farmers Day and Global Fertilizer Day , we should remember a simple truth: Without farmers, there is no fertilizer industry, and without both farmers and the fertilizer industry, there is no reliable source of food. One-half of global food production can be attributed to the use of fertilizer.

Two American industries working together for a common good — even when times are tough.

It’s not an understatement to say that U.S. farmers are facing some of the most difficult economic times in recent history. The latest Department of Agriculture data tell a story farmers already know: Crop producers operated at negative profit margins throughout 2025 and continue to face similar headwinds in 2026 . Interest rates, land rents and input costs remain elevated while commodity receipts have declined for three consecutive years.

The conflict in the Middle East has exposed critical vulnerabilities in the global supply chain and created additional volatility in the global fertilizer market. Damage to fertilizer production facilities and transportation challenges have limited exports from countries that rely on the Strait of Hormuz.

Nearly 50 percent of global exports of sulfur, an important fertilizer, as well as a critical input to phosphate fertilizer production, move through this area. Likewise, between 30 and 50 percent of globally traded nitrogen fertilizer is now unavailable to reach its intended destinations, impacting farmers around the world, including those in the United States.

Regardless of the challenges, the fertilizer industry is deeply committed to supporting America’s farmers, as reflected in the investment decisions individual companies are making in domestic production and in broad support for expanded markets for farm commodities. Without profitable farmers, our industry cannot thrive.

Fertilizer is one of a farmer’s most critical tools to promote plant growth and improve crop yield and productivity, and to ensure farm profitability. When the reliable supply of fertilizers is threatened, the ripple effects are felt in every corner of rural America. For that reason, we believe that a resilient and growing U.S. fertilizer industry is vital to support the American farmer.

Just as U.S. farmers are among the most efficient and innovative in the world, so is the U.S. fertilizer sector. Individual fertilizer producers have publicly announced billions of dollars in new production facilities that help mitigate U.S. agriculture’s exposure to geopolitical disruptions. That’s why the Trump administration’s focus on boosting domestic fertilizer manufacturing is the right policy.

There are more than 100 fertilizer producers globally serving U.S. farmers, and the U.S. is one of only three nations with at least 20 unique companies producing fertilizer products. Still, fertilizer remains a global commodity with 90 percent of consumption occurring outside the United States. The issue is further complicated by the heavy involvement of state-owned entities on the international stage. Demand shocks in Asia or supply disruptions in the Middle East directly affect American farmers.

This reality demands strategic resilience. When geopolitical events disrupt supply corridors, when export restrictions shift commodity flows, when currency swings alter product values overnight, American agriculture should not absorb the full shock of those disruptions. That is why both domestic fertilizer production capacity and global economic stability matter.

Policymakers must understand that fertilizer, food security and agricultural resilience are all interconnected and central to American prosperity. This is not a partisan issue. After all, Republicans and Democrats both depend on American agriculture to put food on their tables.

The path forward requires sound public policy. Farmers, retailers, policymakers and individual companies throughout the fertilizer supply chain each have essential roles. We can build a more resilient foundation by ensuring that policies encourage the expansion of markets for U.S. farm products and create conditions in which individual companies choose to invest in American fertilizer production.

Corey Rosenbusch serves as The Fertilizer Institute’s president and CEO.

articles.title: More home sellers are paying to lower your mortgage rate — and the math can beat a price cut
articles.summary: As high rates discourage prospective homebuyers, sellers are offering creative concessions to get sales done.
articles.body:
Getting a home sold today takes creativity.

Facing a shrinking pool of prospective buyers and some of the highest mortgage rates in three years , motivated sellers are slashing prices and trying new tactics to help lower buyers' financial burdens, like issuing credits to fund mortgage rate buydowns or covering closing costs.

The shift comes as rising mortgage rates and falling home sales give buyers more negotiating power. Mortgage applications have plummeted since late August, and homes are taking longer to sell, contributing to a build-up in available inventory.

Last month, home sellers gave concessions to buyers in more than 45% of all sales, according to Redfin data, the highest share for the month of September since at least 2020. And 22% of sellers dropped prices in the four weeks through Oct. 11.

"I think everyone is just having to get a little bit more creative with the listings and buyers to help make deals work," said Jessica Smith, a real estate agent and founder of the Key Group in Austin, Texas.

Buyers have had the upper hand in Austin for several years, and nearly two-thirds of homes sold there in recent months included some sort of buyer concession, according to Redfin.

Seller concessions cover a broad range of perks for buyers, from prepaying homeowners' association dues to providing cash credits to fund repairs.

But among the most popular concessions today, with mortgage rates hovering at a three-year high of 7.4% , are seller-paid rate buydowns, real estate agents and lenders told Yahoo Finance. In this scenario, a seller agrees to give a buyer a credit toward purchasing discount points, a type of upfront fee that lowers a mortgage rate.

Buydowns can bring a rate down by a set amount for the life of a loan or be structured as a "2/1" buydown, which lowers a mortgage rate by two percentage points for the first year of the loan, then by one percentage point in the second year before reverting to the original agreed-upon rate in year three.

In today's high-rate world, both types can save a buyer far more each month than lowering a home's purchase price by an equivalent amount.

A buyer who put 20% down on a $400,000 home and received $10,000 from their seller to use toward a mortgage rate buydown could permanently reduce their rate to 6.75% and save about $135 a month for the life of their mortgage. A 2/1 buydown would save $418 a month during the first year.

A $10,000 price cut to the home, though, would translate to savings of just $70 a month.

articles.title: Russia sanctions waiver buys time for India but offers no lasting certainty: GTRI
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided temporary relief to
articles.body: US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided temporary relief to India, but the pressure remains as the possibility of Washington restoring the duties is still there according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI).The think tank said on Saturday that while the move eases the immediate threat of fresh trade penalties, the underlying legislation remains in force, allowing the US administration to withdraw the waiver and revive tariff pressure during future trade negotiations."For India, the waiver buys time but offers no lasting certainty. India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed US pressure. Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions," GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said, as quoted by PTI.Trump on Friday signed an executive order implementing the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, while simultaneously suspending certain sanctions and additional duties under the legislation.The law provides for additional tariffs of 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas making fresh purchases from October 18. It also sets out a 500 per cent tariff increase on Russian goods. However, Trump invoked Section 115 of the legislation to waive the duties, citing US national interests."Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order," the executive order stated.The waiver has no fixed expiry date and can be withdrawn. Existing Russia-related sanctions imposed under other executive orders remain unaffected.Why did the US waive the tariffs?GTRI claimed several factors that may have influenced Washington's decision, including its domestic energy requirements, trade arrangements with China and ongoing negotiations with India.According to the think tank, the US agreed on October 9 to purchase Russian diesel to address domestic fuel shortages and elevated prices, making it difficult to justify penalties on other countries for similar purchases. "Punishing other countries for buying Russian energy while doing so itself would invite accusations of double standards," Srivastava said.The report also pointed to Washington's agreement not to raise tariffs on China until January 10, suggesting that imposing additional duties on India alone could complicate bilateral trade negotiations.GTRI noted that Russia's share of India's oil imports declined from 51 per cent in July to 44 per cent in August as Indian refiners increased purchases from the US and the UAE.In the meantime, despite the waiver, the US Trade Representative will continue monitoring Russian energy purchases, leaving Washington with the option of reviewing the relief.You use AI every day. articles.title: America’s $40 trillion debt is coming for your wallet
articles.summary: As the U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion during Donald Trump’s second term, critics warned that escalating interest payments and inflation are eroding public services and devaluing the dollar.
articles.body:
The U.S. national debt recently passed $40 trillion , a number so large that the human brain simply refuses to process it. When President Trump took the oath of office for his second term in January 2025, the balance sheet read $36.2 trillion . Blowing through another nearly $4 trillion in that period of time requires a truly dedicated effort to maxing out the country’s credit cards.

The primary victim of this fiscal blitz is the federal budget itself. The U.S. government now burns more cash servicing the compound interest on past borrowing than it allocates to defending the nation or funding healthcare for millions of citizens. Washington has engineered a financial structure where the state functions primarily as a payout vehicle for global bondholders. Yesterday’s unpaid tabs now consume tomorrow’s public spending. It would be amusing, in an absurd sort of way, if it weren’t so alarming.

While the taxpaying public attempts to digest these incomprehensible figures, the family presiding over the balance sheet appears to be having a good old time. Reports indicate Trump has expanded his personal net worth by $2.2 billion during his second term. His elder sons, Eric and Donald Jr., have joined investment firms , while twenty-year-old Barron Trump reportedly accumulated a $150 million cryptocurrency fortune. Watching an executive family build massive private wealth while the public treasury hemorrhages trillions offers an instructive look at modern priorities.

Politicians across both parties spent decades building this mountain of IOUs, brick by brick. Yet the current velocity breaks every historical precedent on the books. Previous administrations spent decades generating the debt volume that now accumulates in a matter of months. Ongoing military commitments compound the damage daily.

The protracted war with Iran drains tens of billions directly from the treasury, while millions of domestic households struggle to cover basic monthly utility bills.

A towering national debt feels like an abstract accounting game played on balance sheets in Washington, right up until the consequences inevitably spill over into daily life. The federal government has no secret vault of magic gold. It covers its massive interest payments either by gutting domestic services or by creating fresh currency out of thin air. When interest payments devour the federal budget, public health systems lose operational funding. Transport infrastructure falls into disrepair, disaster response agencies run dry mid-season, and critical medical research grinds to a halt.

Printing money to meet existing obligations directly torches purchasing power. The U.S. dollar remains the world’s primary reserve currency. But relentless debt issuance systematically damages its real-world value. When the central bank inflates the overall money supply to keep federal agencies solvent, prices at local grocery stores surge to match the dilution. This process functions as a permanent, non-negotiable tax on every paycheck in the country, without a single vote ever being cast.

The bill for decades of political indulgence has finally arrived, and the political class intends to hand the tab directly to ordinary citizens. Escalating borrowing costs, persistent price inflation, and deteriorating public services aren’t random acts of financial bad luck. Suggesting otherwise is disingenuous in the extreme. Rather, they are the deterministic mathematical outcomes of a government spending capital it doesn’t possess, managed by figures who grow exponentially richer while the public balance sheet burns.

The tragedy of this dynamic lies in its total predictability. Every trillion added to the ledger shifts resources from productive enterprise to debt maintenance. America’s already turgid infrastructure continues to fall further into disrepair. Hospitals face budget cuts while primary dealers collect their yields. The average family works longer hours only to purchase fewer goods, caught in the wake of policy decisions that prioritize immediate political spending over basic economic stability.

Eventually, the limits of continuous borrowing assert themselves in a rather brutal manner. World history contains zero examples of nations spending their way into permanent prosperity on borrowed capital. The illusion of free money persists only as long as global markets accept the underlying currency.

Once that trust disappears, the abstract numbers on Washington spreadsheets become immediate structural hardship for everyday households. Washington accumulates the debt, but ordinary working people pay the invoice through lost wages and degraded public services. The system operates exactly as designed, converting public debt into private advantage while shifting the ultimate risk onto those least equipped to bear it.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: What readers say about taking Social Security at 62
articles.summary: There are many factors to consider about when to start claiming your benefits.
articles.body:
When to start taking Social Security is a hot-button topic, to put it mildly.

My recent column about why so many Americans leave Social Security money on the table resonated with readers.

More than a thousand of you weighed in about what you did or plan to do.

The size of your Social Security check depends on your work history, lifetime earnings, retirement age, and the year you start claiming benefits.

You can begin receiving your Social Security benefit as early as age 62, but doing so reduces the dollar amount by as much as 30% from what it would have been at your full retirement age (FRA). For anyone born in 1960 or later, your full retirement age is 67.

If you push back benefits from your full retirement age until age 70, you earn delayed retirement credits. Those come to roughly an 8% increase for each year until you hit 70, when the credits stop accruing.

More than a quarter of Social Security beneficiaries begin claiming benefits at age 62, as soon as they're eligible, and only a small percentage wait until they hit 70, often because they are still on the job and don't need the money to live on.

Social Security monthly payments account for at least half the income of close to 24 million older adults. The average monthly benefit is around $2,000 a month, or about $25,000 a year. For roughly 12% of men and 15% of women 65 or older, nearly all their living expenses, including housing costs, are paid from their Social Security.

Most financial advisers and retirement experts agree that for lots of folks, delaying their benefit until age 70, if they can afford to, will deliver a larger monthly check for the rest of their lives.

Let's agree on one thing — there is no single right age for claiming Social Security.

Based on the comments I received, most people want the money right now to enjoy it or invest it. They worry they won't live long enough to receive the bigger checks if they delay.

The following is an edited sample of those comments — and my take on them. Feel free to weigh in, of course, in the comments section at the end.

Assuming a 7% return on the additional money, my break even point is at age 86 if starting my SSA at 62. I don't feel like I am leaving money on the table. Completely the opposite. The money left on the table would be if I should perish before I even see any money.

My break-even age at which waiting would be the smarter choice is 79, which is about the current average life expectancy in the US. Even if you are blessed and live the average additional 20 years for a 62-year old, why roll the dice? Also, you will never enjoy the money more than you will at 62, 63, 64, etc.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: For the first time since Covid, the leisure and spiritual destinations — Ranthambore and Rishikesh — have been overtaken by Mumbai and Delhi as the Indian cities with highest average hotel tariffs. articles.body:
MapQuest added a new feature to its mobile app Thursday that allows users to turn on a “surveillance layer” to find known license plate readers in their route.

“The Roads Have Eyes!,” MapQuest said on social platform Bluesky Thursday announcing the new feature.

“Turn on the Surveillance Layer in Map Options to see known license plate readers from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada, and other outdoor surveillance cameras,” the post read.

Earlier this month, progressive lawmakers introduced legislation to ban federal agencies from using automatic license plate readers (ALPRs). The Ban Flock Act would stop federal agencies from using ALPR and pause federal grant funding to state and local governments with ALPR contracts.

The legislation would also allow Americans to sue the federal government for the use of ALPRs.

One of the ALPR firms, Flock Safety, took the center stage in a controversy earlier this year for its network of more than 120,000 cameras across the country.

Flock’s plate readers not only record license plate numbers, but specific details about a car to create what the company calls a “vehicle signature.” The details include the make, model and color of the car along with unique features like bumper stickers, decals, and accessories. The company, however, does not use biometric data or facial recognition.

A series of recent reports shed light on multiple instances of law enforcement misusing Flock or other ALPRs. Among those is a Washington Post investigation that found more than 50 officers had been accused, charged with or convicted of misusing Flock or other license plate readers to spy on exes or romantic interests.

Last month, a bipartisan pair of senators sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche, urging him to disclose details about any use of ALPRs by the Justice Department. Sens. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) and Katie Britt (R-Ala.) also requested the issuance of guidance to state and local law enforcement agencies to prevent the misuse of ALPRs.

Andrew Smith, a Flock spokesperson, told The Hill in a statement that the company “strongly supports legislation establishing guardrails governing license plate reader use.”

MapQuest’s popularity surged last month after the company announced that it would not rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America” after President Trump signed an executive order changing its name. The company said following the announcement, its mobile app received hundreds of thousands of downloads.

The company also responded similarly in 2025 to Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” on his first day back in office. MapQuest allowed its users to refer to the body of water however they wanted.

articles.body:
Recent data paints a bleak picture of the economy , lending Republicans another blow as midterm early-voting is underway.

Annual inflation, as measured by the consumer price index (CPI), rose from 3.4 percent in August to 3.7 percent in September , the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported Wednesday.

A day later, the BLS reported that wholesale prices in September experienced their highest monthly jump in more than four years.

The GOP, who are already saddled with President Trump’s unpopularity and an Iran war that is increasing costs, now look for a way to flip the economy’s script.

“It’s a continuation of bad news, confirming what voters are telling us every day of what they’re experiencing,” Republican strategist Doug Heye told The Hill.

In the last election cycle, Trump and Republicans campaigned on lowering the cost of essentials after inflation soared to a 40-year high under former President Joe Biden.

But inflation, as measured by the CPI, rebounded under Biden to 3 percent in January 2025. Since then, it has increased by 0.7 percentage points and reached the highest point since May last month.

“There were pre-existing problems, no doubt about it, but they’ve been exacerbated proactively by the president, and so that’s why Republicans find themselves where they are,” argued Heye, who is also a former communications director of the Republican National Committee.

Polling shows that voters blame Trump for persistent inflation, with roughly six in 10 respondents to a recent Associated Press-NORC survey saying the economy was worse off since the president returned to office.

Nearly 51 percent of respondents to a NewsNation and Decision Desk HQ poll, The Hill’s partners, conducted earlier this month said they are casting their midterm ballot to “oppose” Trump and his policies.

Jim Kessler, the executive vice president for policy at the center-left think tank Third Way, said the latest economic data only makes life harder for Republicans.

“If the numbers had come in a lot better both in September and October on inflation, and the Trump administration had something to say, then people might feel that things are turning around,” Kessler told The Hill.

Democrats have pounced on the data as they seek control of Congress for the next chunk of Trump’s term.

Democrats on the congressional Joint Economic Committee released a report this week showing that gas price spikes amid the Iran war have cost the average American family $856.

“Instead of the relief President Trump promised, his war, tariffs, and other reckless policies continue to make it harder for families to afford the basics,” said Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), the ranking member of the committee.

Hassan’s focus on cost-of-living concerns tracks with what Democrats around the country are saying ahead of Election Day.

Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright told The Hill on Friday his party is “unified” around affordability for the first time in his lifetime.

“All of them are talking about gas prices. Most of them are talking about … the high cost of living,” added Seawright, an adviser to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and Democratic National Committee.

“We are not only identifying the problem, but we’re offering the solutions to the problems that Republicans have created,” he added.

Kessler traced the messaging shift from Democrats to last year’s record-long government shutdown , which stemmed from the party pushing for an extension of since-expired Affordable Care Act premium subsidies .

During that funding lapse, Democrats’ focus “got tighter” and focused on “the things that the average voter cares about,” he said.

“The most important thing about an election is to listen to voters and to reflect what they’re feeling, not to tell them what they ought to feel and what they ought to care about,” Kessler added.

Trump and Republicans have sought to turn the tide, accusing Democrats of being “communists” after multiple left-wing candidates won primaries earlier this year — also pointing fingers at the Biden administration.

Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council, told NewsNation’s Hannah Brandt this week that Americans “were worse off” due to the former Democratic president’s policies.

Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee added that “President Trump and Republicans are working to lower costs and repair the damage Democrats left behind after years of reckless spending.”

“Democrats can campaign on the pain they helped create, but Republicans are focused on lowering the cost of living, cutting taxes, and putting more money back in Americans’ pockets,” Marinella said.

Prices, notably for gas, diesel and fertilizer, have risen since the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war. While the conflict continues, Trump has attempted to address the economic spillover effects, recently touting a deal with Russia to increase that country’s supply of diesel fuel to the global marketplace.

But gas and diesel prices remain significantly above pre-war totals. The average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly $4.33 as of Friday, while diesel costs $6.33 per gallon, according to AAA .

A year ago, a gallon of gas and diesel cost about $3.06 and $3.65 on average, respectively, per AAA.

Wholesale energy prices rose by 10.8 percent from August to September, the BLS reported this week. That was higher than the 10.5-percent increase in March, the first month of the war, and indicates energy markets are still feeling the squeeze.

Seawright, though, argued that the Iran war “just put a bow” on the difficult economic picture for the GOP, citing Trump’s tariffs.

Heye also faulted Trump for Republicans’ midterm prospects, claiming Democrats have not “needed” to effectively capitalize on the landscape given how a majority of Americans view the president.

“The reality is, when you have a president whose approval rating’s at 36 percent three weeks before the vote … if you’re running against that, you’re in pretty good shape,” Heye said.
